blocks.text: Arrays are fast and simple, so why invent anything else? Because arrays have one big weakness: their elements must sit **side by side**. Whenever you add or remove something anywhere except the end, the neighbours have to move. Linked lists exist to remove that cost.

Say you have `[10, 20, 30, 40]` and want to put `5` at the **front**. In an array there is no empty slot at index 0 — so every element has to move one place to the right first. Four elements means four moves; a million elements means a million moves.

blocks.text: The linked list way: change one arrow

In a linked list, nothing has to move. Create a new node anywhere in memory, point it at the old head, and call it the new head. That's **two pointer changes**, whether the list has 4 nodes or 4 million.

blocks.code:
def insert_at_head(head, x):
    node = ListNode(x)
    node.next = head   # point the new node at the old head
    return node        # it is the new head

blocks.text: An array is created with a fixed amount of room. When it fills up, a growable array (JavaScript arrays, Python lists, Java's `ArrayList`, C++'s `vector`) has to grab a **bigger block** and **copy every element** into it. A linked list never runs out of room in that way: each new node is just one more small allocation.

blocks.alt: Left: a full array of capacity 4 being copied into a new array of capacity 8 to make room. Right: a linked list simply gains one more node at the end.

blocks.text: Linked lists aren't free. The same arrows that make inserting cheap cause three costs:

items: **No jumping to an index.** `arr[500]` is instant; reaching the 500th node means following 500 arrows — **O(n)**.
**Extra memory.** Every node stores a pointer alongside its value — on a 64-bit machine that's 8 extra bytes per element, often more than the value itself.
**Slower to scan in practice.** Array elements sit next to each other, so the CPU loads many at once into its cache. Nodes are scattered, so each hop can be a slow trip to main memory.

blocks.text: Arrays vs linked lists at a glance

blocks.alt: A comparison table. Access by index: array O(1), linked list O(n). Insert or delete at the front: array O(n), list O(1). Insert or delete in the middle once you are there: array O(n), list O(1). Search: both O(n). Extra memory per element: array none, list one pointer.

items: Arrays must keep elements side by side, so inserting or deleting near the front shifts everything: **O(n)**.
A linked list just rewires arrows: inserting or deleting at a node you already hold is **O(1)**.
Linked lists grow one node at a time — no big copy when they "fill up".
The trade-off: no O(1) indexing, extra memory per node, and less cache-friendly scanning.
